To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have developed novel opioid receptor models and applied them to the rational design of novel opioid receptor ligands.
we have developed a new class of opioid ligands, which are highly potent and selective at MOR and DOR, but with low affinity for KOR.

1) the structure of the MOR and the KOR can be used to rationally design ligands with desired functional properties, and 2) subtle structural variations in a pentapeptide ligand can result in dramatic changes in receptor affinity and function.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of novel opioid receptor modulators with the aim of improving the therapeutic profile of current MOR agonists by targeting the MOR/DOR system.
the development of novel ligands for the opioid receptors.

the design and synthesis of opioid receptor ligands that are selective for the mu opioid receptor, with a particular focus on ligands that are agonists at MOR, antagonists at delta opioid receptors, and devoid of kappa opioid receptor activity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the use of accurate active‐ and inactive‐state receptor models, in conjunction with the appropriate computational methods, can be used to rationally design ligands with tailored receptor selectivity and functional activity.
the present study demonstrates the power and utility, and also the limitations, of accurate receptor models in ligand design.
the present study has shown that a combination of a MOR agonistic and DOR antagonistic peptide is a promising candidate for future in vivo investigations of MOR/DOR interaction.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the active state receptor model is a better model for agonist design and the inactive state receptor model is the better model for antagonist design.
the structure of the peptide backbone is critical to the functional properties of these peptides.
the structure‐function relationship for opioid ligands has been clarified, and the design of ligands for the MOR, DOR, and KOR has been advanced.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it demonstrates how the use of active and inactive state receptor models can be used to design ligands with tailored affinity and functional profiles.
it is possible to design ligands that have tailored affinity and efficacy for multiple receptors, and this can be achieved by using active or inactive state models of the receptor.
the receptor models can be used to guide the design of ligands with the desired pharmacological profile.
